REMARKS/ARGUMENTS
Summary of the Office Action
The Office Action dated April 15, 2024 (the “Office Action”) contains the following objections and rejections: Claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being indefinite Claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 for being directed to an abstract idea Claims 1 and 17 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(l) as being anticipated by Benzel et al (U.S. Publication No. 2012/0220893) Claim 4 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Benzel in view of Kuo et al (U.S. Publication No. 2017/0156635) Claims 5-7, 21, 25-27, and 37 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Benzel in view of Howard et al (U.S. Patent No. 9,129,499) Claim 11 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Benzel in view of Kirovski et al (U.S. Patent No. 8,761,437) Claim 14 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Benzel in view of Gonzales et al (U.S. Publication No. 2017 /0238850) Claim 24 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Benzel and Howard, as applied to claim 21 above, and further in view of Kuo Claim 31 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Benzel and Howard, as applied to claim 21 above, and further in view of Kirovski Claim 34 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Benzel and Howard, as applied to claim 21 above, and further in view of Gonzales
Summary of the Amendments
Claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33, and 37 are pending. By this response, claims 1, 5-8, 14, 21, 25-28, and 34 are amended. Claims 4, 17, 24, and 37 are cancelled. New claims 81-84 are added. Support for the amendments and new claims can be found within the originally filed claims and throughout the Specification, and at least within paragraphs 0063, 0064, 0065, 0070, 0071, 0078, 0079, 0084, 0085, 0097. No new matter is added by this response.
Claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 are Definite
The Office Action rejected claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly being indefinite for “insufficient antecedent basis” for several terms. Applicant amends the terms as follows: Claim 1 is amended to recite “a head.” Claim 7 is amended to recite “a brain.” Claim 8 is amended to delete the terms “the following equation,” “(the mass),” and “(the base).” Claim 8 is amended to recite “a moment,” “a mass,” “a stiffness,” “angles,” “a brain,” “a skull,” and “a base.” Claim 13 is amended to delete the term “the following logistic model.” Claim 13 is amended to recite “a probability,” “components,” “an injury criterion,” “fitted coefficients” and “a number of anatomical directions.” Claim 21 is amended to recite “a head,” “a computer system,” and “a brain angle metric.” Claim 25 is amended to recite “the brain angle metric.” Claim 28 is amended to delete the terms “the following equation,” “(the mass),” and “(the base).” Claim 27 is amended to recite “a brain.” Claim 28 is amended to recite “a moment,” “a mass,” “a stiffness,” “angles,” “a brain,” “a skull,” and “a base.” Claim 33 is amended to delete the term “the following logistic model.” .” Claim 33 is amended to recite “a probability,” “components,” “an injury criterion,” “fitted coefficients” and “a number of anatomical directions.”
Based on the foregoing, claims 1, 7, 8, 13, 21, 25, 27, 28, and 33 and its dependents should be found to be definite. Application respectfully request that the rejection of claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 for being indefinite be withdrawn.
Claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 are Directed to Eligible Subject Matter
The Office Action rejected claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 for allegedly being directed to an abstract idea without significantly more. In particular, the Office Action alleges that claim 1 recites “an abstract idea that is part of the Mathematical Concepts and/or Mental Processes group.” Applicant respectfully disagrees as claim 1 is directed to a real-time system for assessment of head impacts kinematics and detection of concussive events. This system is both a particular machine and improves a technology. Accordingly, claim 1 is subject matter eligible under step 2A prong 2 as being directed to the practical application that is implemented with a particular machine. Claim 1 is also subject matter eligible under step 2A prong 2 as being directed to the practical application that improves detection of concussive events.
Claim 1 is directed to a particular machine
Claim 1 is directed to a particular system comprising particular elements. The system comprises a head-mounted device and a computer system. The head-mounted device is configured to be worn or secured to a head. The device comprises one or more accelerators for capturing brain angle measurements when fitted onto the head of an individual. The device is in communication with a computer system for real time analysis. The computer system directs the accelerators to capture the brain angle measurements. The computer system then utilizes the measurements as input into a model to detect concussive events in real time. The combination head-mounted device, one or more accelerometers, and a computational system for directing the capture of measurements for real-time detection of concussive events cannot be considered a generic computer. Instead, these are particular components required to perform particular tasks and work in concert to detect concussive events in real time.
As claimed, the head-mounted device and accelerometers are not a mere extra-solution activity of field-of-use but are integral to the real-time detection of concussive events. The accelerometers are required to capture brain angle measurements. The accelerometers must be comprised as part of the head-mounted device such that it can detect angular head motion. And the computer system directs the accelerometers to capture the brain angle measurements and compute a brain angle metric that is utilized to distinguish whether an impact was a concussive event or a non-concussive event in real time.
Claim 1 comprises particular elements that are integrated together to perform real time detection of concussive events. The elements, especially in combination, are not generic, an extra-solution activity, or a mere field-of-use. Claim 1 is subject matter eligible under step 2A prong 2 for being directed to a particular machine.
Claim 21 is directed to a method of use of claim 1’s system for real-time detection of concussive events. Accordingly, claim 21 is also subject matter eligible under step 2A prong 2 for being directed to the use of a particular machine.
Claim 1 improves a technology
Claim 1 improves the technology of concussion detection. The solution provided by claim 1 detects concussive events using simplified computation that can facilitate faster and better detection of concussive events, as compared to the finite element models of the prior art. And claim 1 directed to the use rotational acceleration, which is better correlated with brain trauma severity than translational acceleration. These benefits are highlighted in the Specification:
Diffuse brain injury, which can occur through purely inertial head acceleration even in the absence of skull deformation, has become better understood since the development of HIC and SI. Rapid head rotations can shear and deform the white matter of the brain causing diffuse axonal injury (DAI), a fundamentally different injury than focal injuries caused by skull deformation which are primarily caused by translational motions. Indeed, while head translational acceleration is an important factor for focal trauma such as skull fracture, rotational acceleration causes time-dependent inertial loading of the brain and better correlates with brain trauma severity in animal experiments . More recently, NHTSA
developed the brain injury criterion (BrIC) to predict TBI risk by relating head rotational velocity to critical brain strains; this criterion has been proposed to be used in the New Car Assessment Programs rating (Takhounts, E.G., Craig, M.J., Moorhouse, K., Mcfadden, J., and Hasija, V. (2013). Stapp Car Crash J. 57, 1–24, the disclosure of which is incorporated herein by reference). Realizing that both translational and rotational head kinematics may factor into injury risk, some 6 degree-of-freedom (DOF) criteria such as head impact power (HIP) and generalized acceleration model for brain injury threshold (GAMBIT) have also been developed, which include both translational and rotational components of acceleration. Brain tissue deformation metrics calculated from finite element (FE) simulations are another category of frequently investigated injury criteria (for more HIP, see Newman, J.A., Shewchenko, N., and Welbourne, E. (2000) Stapp Car Crash J. 44, 362; for more on GAMBIT, see Newman, J. (1986). Proc. Int. Res. Counc. Biokinetics Impacts, 121–131; the disclosures of which are each incorporated herein by reference). Using these FE models, researchers simulate metrics such as tissue strain and strain rate to predict injury risk. Morphologically-based metrics such as fiber tract-oriented strain, which better accounts for anisotropy in brain tissue, have also been found to correlate with injury (see Sahoo, D., Deck, C., and Willinger, R. (2016). Accid. Anal. Prev. 92, 53–70, the disclosure of which is incorporated herein by reference). Although finite element model-derived criteria provide more physical intuition behind injury risk prediction than skull-kinematics based criteria, they are severely limited by long computational running time and may not be practical options as federal standards.
Specification, ¶ 0108, emphasis added
The system of claim 1 does not require 6 degree-of-freedom (DOF) criteria or both translational and rotational components of acceleration. Instead, the method is directed to the computation a brain angle metric using less intensive computation that requires only angular head motion. This system reduces the amount of computation time to yield a more practical solution to detecting concussive events, as protocols to detect concussive events would perform computation on multiple head movements to assess whether each movement was a concussive event. This benefit magnified when utilized in situations involving a lot of repeated head movements, such as sports and combat.
The method also yielded improved accuracy and sensitivity in detection of concussive events as compared to prior methods such as the 6DOF head impact power (HIP), HIP separated into each direction (HIP3D), generalized acceleration model for brain injury threshold (GAMBIT), and the Virginia Tech combined probability metric (VTCP):

Claim 1 is directed to a system that requires less computation time and yields improved accuracy and sensitivity in detection of concussive events. Claim 1 is subject matter eligible under step 2A prong 2 for being directed to a system that improves a technology.
Claim 21 is directed to a method of use of claim 1’s system for real-time detection of concussive events. Accordingly, claim 21 is also subject matter eligible under step 2A prong 2 for being directed to the use a system that improves a technology.
Based on the foregoing, Applicant provides that claims 1 and 21 are directed to eligible subject matter. Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 for being directed to ineligible subject matter be withdrawn.
Claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 are Novel and Patentable
The Office Action rejected claims 1 and 17 under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) as allegedly being anticipated by Benzel et al (U.S. Publication No. 2012/0220893). The Office Action further rejected claims 5-7, 21, 25-27, and 37 under 35 U.S.C. 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Benzel in view of Howard et al (U.S. Patent No. 9,129,499). All other dependent claims were also rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over a various combinations of Benzel and other citations or Benzel, Howard and other citations. Applicant respectfully disagrees and provides further clarification on the differences between the claims and the cited references. Applicant submits that independent claims 1 and 21, when interpreted as whole, are novel and patentable.
The M.P.E.P. holds “A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference” (M.P.E.P., § 2131). A claim is patentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if the differences between the claimed invention and prior art, when interpreted as a whole, would be unobvious as determined by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time filing (M.P.E.P. § 2141).
The Office Action cites the Benzel reference for anticipating claim 1. Without acquiescing to the correctness of such citation, Applicant has amended claim 1 to recite “obtain brain angle measurements … from the one or more accelerometers for measuring angular head motion …; compute, utilizing a brain angle measurement and a mathematical mass-spring-damper model, a brain angle metric.” The Benzel reference does not teach or render obvious the capturing brain angle measurements or utilizing those measurements to compute a brain angle metric. Claim 1 is novel over of the Benzel reference.
The Office Action also cites the Howard reference to establish a teaching of “a mass-spring-damper model (Column 31 Line 17 - Column 32 Line 5).” Applicant notes that Howard is utilizing a physical system that includes a physical mass, physical springs, and physical dampers. Claims 1 and 21 as amended (and prior claims 6 and 26) were directed towards mathematical mass-spring-damper models that are nonphysical, as can be readily interpreted by the Specification and further claims, which clearly recite the mass-spring-damper models as equations. A person having ordinary skill in the art would not find that the broadest reasonable interpretation of the mass-spring-damper model described in the Specification would include a physical model. For instance, a person of ordinary skill in the art would not find it be reasonable for a physical mass, physical springs, and physical dampers to compute a kinematic metric when these machineries have no computational ability. In any regard, the claims have been amended to recite a “mathematical mass-spring-damper model” throughout to clear any ambiguity.
The Howard reference also does not render the use of a mathematical mass-spring-damper model as obvious. The reference provides no teaching or suggestion that a brain angle measurement captured from one or more accelerometers can be utilized as input in a mass-spring-damper model to compute a brain angle metric. It is unclear how the physical system of the Howard reference would be utilized to compute a brain angle metric, as there is no teaching within the Howard reference on how to use of the physical system to compute any angle metric. The Office Action further does not provide any rationale for why Howard’s physical system teaches of computing a brain angle metric. The Action merely states that “the head kinematic metric is a brain angle metric that is computed utilizing a mass-deformation brain model” but fails to describe how the Howard physical system computes the brain angle metric and or even which brain metric is computed by the physical system. Because of the lack any mention of computing brain angle measurements from Howard’s physical model, a person having ordinary skill in the art would not interpret the Howard reference to provide any teaching or suggestion that a brain angle measurement is captured from one or more accelerometers to be utilized as input in a mass-spring-damper model to compute a brain angle metric. As such, the claims 1 and 21 cannot be considered unpatentable over the combination of Benzel and Howard references. And none of the other cited references make up for the deficiencies of the Benzel and Howard references.
Based on the foregoing, Applicant provides that claims 1 and 21 and their dependents are novel and patentable. Applicant respectfully requests that the prior art rejections of claims 1, 4-8, 11, 13-14, 17, 21, 24-28, 31, 33-34, and 37 over the cited references be withdrawn.
Conclusion
In view of the foregoing amendments and remarks, it is respectfully submitted that this application is in condition for allowance. Accordingly, reconsideration of the application and allowance of the claims are respectfully requested. Although the present paper may include a combination of alterations to the application or claims, or characterizations of claim scope or referenced art, Applicant is not conceding that previously pending claims in this application are not patentable over the cited references. Rather, any alterations and/or characterizations are made to strictly facilitate prosecution of this application. As such, reviewers of this or any parent, child, or related prosecution history shall not reasonably infer that Applicant has made any disclaimers or disavowals of any subject matter supported by the present application.
Applicant has submitted amendments and arguments believed to be sufficient to overcome all of the outstanding rejections. Consequently, Applicant has not advanced every argument for the allowability of the claims over the references of record. As such, Applicant does not acquiesce to any of the Examiner's statements or characterizations not specifically traversed. If the Examiner should have any remaining questions or objections, a telephone interview to discuss and resolve these issues is respectfully requested.
The Commissioner is authorized to charge any fee under 37 CFR 1.16 and 1.17 that may be required during the entire pendency of the application to Deposit Account No. 50-4407. Please show our docket number with any transaction to the Deposit Account.
